prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I opened with active-matter hydrodynamics (B009) and still think it is the cleanest example of a simple, universal mechanism on the list. But after reading the ballots I am putting magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for this configuration. It has the structure I value most: a compact analytical model (Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum theory) that says where to look, followed by an experiment (Jarillo-Herrero's group, 2018) that finds correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. Theory and experiment reinforce each other, the result has been reproduced independently and extended into a whole family of moire systems, and four of the five members who ranked it placed it in their top three. The three-name credit fits the theory-plus-experiment pairing without forcing an artificial cut.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is maturity. The discovery is eight years old and the pairing mechanism of the superconductivity is unsettled, so one could argue that the prize would be rewarding a platform whose lasting physics has not yet been identified. Attribution is also imperfect: Yuan Cao and the other first authors of the 2018 papers are not in the credited names, and the experimental half rests on a group leader. Finally B009 has had only my support, so putting B047 first risks looking like a compromise rather than a judgement about which discovery is most fundamental.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B047 fifth and proposed only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. He considers it somewhat premature because the superconductivity is not understood, and he thinks Bistritzer's role is real but could be left out.
responses.response: I agree about the superconductivity, but I do not think the prize needs a mechanism for it. The discovery is the existence of correlated and superconducting phases at the predicted flat-band angle, which has been reproduced widely. I disagree with dropping Bistritzer: the magic-angle result is the Bistritzer-MacDonald paper, and a prize that credits the prediction should name both authors. The union fits within three people, so there is no space argument for omitting him. I would accept that the credit for the experimental side is thin, but that is a different problem.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B047 first. She sees the transport experiments as the original observation, the Bistritzer-MacDonald theory as the guide to where to look, and the lasting impact across moire materials as large.
responses.response: I largely agree with her, and I put more weight than she does on the theory. The experiment was a search at a specific angle because the continuum model predicted flat bands there, so I would not word the citation as an experimental discovery alone. Her point that other device and fabrication coauthors complicate the credit is the honest weak spot, and I would want the committee to check the 2018 author contributions before settling on Jarillo-Herrero as the sole experimental name.

responses.point: Johansson ranked circuit QED (B004) first and B047 third. He sees the twisted-graphene interpretation as only partly stable, with twist-angle disorder complicating reproducibility, and notes that timing may be early.
responses.response: The twist-angle disorder point is correct, and sample-to-sample variation is a genuine limit on quantitative claims. But the qualitative result, flat bands plus correlated and superconducting phases, has survived across many groups, including fractional Chern insulators that were found later. That seems a stronger test of stability than the exact superconducting dome. On B004 I defer to him on the physics. My hesitation there is only that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close, and I would want to understand how distinct the committee thinks strong coupling is from that work.

responses.point: Kroll ranked optical lattice clocks (B019) first, as a decisive gain in measurement precision with a clean two-person credit and strong independent confirmation.
responses.response: I agree B019 is mature, clean and well attributed, which is why I keep it as an alternative. My reservation is the question of what is discovered: a long programme of systematic improvement on top of the frequency comb is an instrument achievement, while B047 is a new regime of matter. That is a matter of the prize's emphasis, not a strong disagreement, and I would not object if the committee preferred B019 for its maturity.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the three-name credit given that Yuan Cao and other first authors of the 2018 experiments are outside the credited names.
Whether the superconducting mechanism has to be settled before the prize is timely.
Yuhai Tu's absence from the B009 credit leaves Toner-Tu hydrodynamics with a real attribution gap, which is why I did not keep B009 as the preferred configuration.
How strongly the committee weighs the broader consensus, since B009 has only my support and I have no independent check on how other members would assess it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for any shortlisted ballot. I have no recorded collaboration with the credited names. Eva Olsson and Goran Johansson are in the neighbouring Chalmers environment, but no specific collaboration or conflict is apparent.
